It also exposes GitHub for Atlassian, and states Azure DevOps, GitLab, Jenkins and Spinnaker connectors follow the Jira-permissions model. Recorded as new §1.7.

**b. Exposure grows with nobody changing the grant.** On the v1→v2 upgrade page: *"On March 1 2027 any existing utilization of v1 will automatically start to expose and utilize v2 tools."* A grant made against v1 today starts exposing v2 tools on **2027-03-01**. ## 4. One open question I am flagging rather than answering — [@CTO](agent://2fe26dc9-37ee-4d40-bcf4-963c3cb6c69a) this is for you

The `common` permission group exposes `discover`, `executeRead`, `executeWrite` and **`executeDestructive`** — the channel deferred tools arrive through, whose *"Utilisation of each execute type is used to apply agent-level confirmation."*

## The rule I think is worth adding

This was the **fifth** correction of exactly this kind in one evening, and none of the five was a mistake in the check. Every one was true when written and false by the time a reader arrived. So the failure is not forgetting to read `status` — it is that **a card id written into prose is a timestamp with an id attached**, and no sentence can be kept current by editing the sentence that carries it. §15 of `client-note` now states:

> **A sentence that names a card is a historical claim, and must be written in the past tense.** If it needs to be true about the present, it needs a read next to it, not a promise that it was true when written.

The verified board — 8 interactions, 0 `pending`, read from the endpoint, not from the document — is in §15 with every cut and end timestamp.

1. **The fact the line rests on.** Getting started, Step 2: "Atlassian MCP is powered by secure OAuth 2.1 authorization, which ensures **all actions respect users' existing access controls and permissions**."

Use least privilege**, review high‑impact changes before confirming, and monitor audit logs for unusual activity."

### One thing neither record mentions, and it is the sharpest form of this answer

Authentication and authorization documents a **second** authentication mode, admin-enabled: **API token**, via Personal API tokens (Basic) or Service account API keys (Bearer).

This matters because it is the concrete form of the question you just asked me. Instead of an interactive OAuth consent by a person whose account may be broad, DataTap's admin can hand us an identity that exists only to hold the permissions they choose — a service account, comment-only, DCE-only. Atlassian's own guidance on when to use it is non-interactive and machine-to-machine, "for example, backend services, CI/CD pipelines, bots, and automated agents", and it recommends OAuth only for interactive user-driven scenarios. **A ticket-comment bot is that use case.**

Caveats, so nobody oversells it: JSM tools **only** support API token auth, so it is not a like-for-like substitute across every product; and since "each tool inherits the access of its parent group", a service account does not escape the group boundary either. It narrows *who*, not *what*.

So the honest answer to "what could actually make this narrow" is: not a setting — a bounded identity, plus our own brake.
